name: Sciton BBL / Moxi / Halo
lead: BBL, Moxi and Halo are clinic treatments performed on laser and light platforms made by Sciton. BBL (BroadBand Light) is an intense pulsed light treatment, Moxi is a fractionated 1927-nm laser, and Halo is a dual-wavelength 2940/1470-nm hybrid fractional laser, as described in registered studies.[1] People have them to improve skin tone and texture: BBL targets sun-related pigment and redness, Moxi targets surface pigmentation and photodamage, and Halo works deeper on texture, pores and scars. Clinics sometimes combine all three in one session.[1]

The published record is made up of small studies. A completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for skin pigment[1], a split-face study compared IPL with pulsed dye laser for facial erythema[2], a 2023 study examined a fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes[3], and a split-face randomized trial examined broadband light for enlarged facial pores[9]. Many older papers on Sciton-type devices concern erbium:YAG resurfacing.

chain: BBL light is absorbed by pigment and blood vessels
Moxi and Halo create microscopic columns of controlled injury
Skin renews and remodels with a more even tone and smoother surface
angle.text: These are professional treatments people book to even out sun spots, redness, texture and scars. BBL works through light absorption, while the fractional lasers stimulate skin renewal in a pattern of tiny columns.

paras: BBL is a broadband, non-laser light source of the intense pulsed light (IPL) type. IPL uses a xenon flashlamp that emits brief pulses of non-coherent light across a broad range of wavelengths, with filters that block unwanted wavelengths so the energy is absorbed by chromophores such as melanin and haemoglobin; the absorbed energy heats and destroys the target, such as pigmented cells or small blood vessels.[4] IPL is attributed to Shimon Eckhouse, who invented it in 1992, with the first systems reaching the market in 1995 and clearances for pigmented lesions and hair removal following in 1996 and 1997.[4]

A split-face comparison found IPL could be used in place of pulsed dye laser, the historical standard, for reducing facial erythema.[2] A split-face randomized trial examined broadband light for enlarged facial pores,[9] and a split-face trial paired botulinum toxin with broadband light for erythematotelangiectatic rosacea.[10] A combination of broadband light and intradermal tranexamic acid has been studied for chloasma.[11]

In a split-face randomized trial of 25 patients who received five BBL treatments two weeks apart, total pore count measured with VISIA imaging was 801 on treated sides versus 812 on untreated sides two months later, a difference that was not statistically significant, and no long-term side effects were reported; the authors described BBL as safe and mildly effective for pores. [9][17]

Moxi is described in registered studies as a fractionated 1927-nm laser for pigmentation and photodamage.[1][3] Fractionated resurfacing treats a pattern of microscopic columns and leaves surrounding skin intact, which supports faster healing than treating the whole surface. The 1927-nm wavelength is absorbed strongly by water in the upper skin layers, so its effect is concentrated near the surface.

In a 2023 prospective study in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine, 27 women (mean age 47, Fitzpatrick skin types I to IV) received two fractionated nonablative 1927-nm treatments one month apart; spots, UV spots and brown spots decreased significantly at one month, brown spots remained improved at three months, and clinician global assessment scores averaged 3.4 and 3.7 at one and three months, which the authors describe as roughly 50 percent improvement in hyperpigmentation. [3][16] No serious adverse events occurred, and the authors suggest pigment gains may fade with later sun exposure, so repeat treatments may be needed to maintain results. [3][16]

Halo is described as a dual-wavelength 2940/1470 nm hybrid fractional laser, combining an ablative erbium wavelength with a non-ablative one.[1][5] A recruiting trial evaluates a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in patients with skin of colour.[5] Related research on fractional ablative lasers has reported skin tightening linked to closure of the laser-created holes.[8]

Sciton's website lists the company's headquarters in Palo Alto, California, and presents BBL, Moxi and Halo as handpieces and attachments for its JOULE and mJOULE platforms, with product variants such as Super Moxi, Halo TriBrid and BBL HEROic. [18] Because the three modalities run on one platform, a single clinic visit can combine them, which is the basis of the combined protocol registered in a small pilot. [1]

Layering light and laser treatments is a recurring theme in the literature. A completed trial registered the combined BBL, Moxi and Halo protocol for pigment,[1] another trial paired a placebo moisturiser with a non-ablative laser for facial photoaging, discoloration and texture,[6] and a small registered study used a BBL-type light source to activate a topical photodynamic agent for actinic keratoses and photodamage.[12] Journal reports describe combination ablative approaches to advanced facial ageing.[13]

IPL is generally considered safe, but complications such as hyperpigmentation can occur, and photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are listed as contraindications; one comparison reported temporary side effects in about 15 percent of patients.[4] Studies of ablative erbium and CO2 resurfacing report differences in healing time and side-effect rates, and trials of wound dressings after laser resurfacing show that post-procedure care is an active area of study.[7][14] Laser-induced hyperpigmentation is listed as a condition in one registered trial.[5]

A completed 15-participant trial combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment (NCT06091215), a 38-participant phase 4 trial examined a moisturiser with a non-ablative laser for photoaging, and a 5-participant study evaluated infrared and broadband light for skin ageing.[1][6][15] A study of fractionated 1927-nm laser reported on diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes.[3] A randomized split-face trial of broadband light for enlarged pores and a split-face trial of IPL versus pulsed dye laser for erythema are also published.[2][9] Single-pass CO2 and multiple-pass Er:YAG resurfacing were directly compared for healing and side effects in an older trial.[7] Sample sizes are small, and the registry entries do not summarise results. The 27-patient Moxi study found significant reductions in brown spots at one month, and the 25-patient split-face pore trial did not find a significant difference between BBL-treated and untreated sides. [16][17]

timeline.event: Shimon Eckhouse invents intense pulsed light.[4]
IPL is introduced to the medical market and approved by the FDA for vascular lesions.[4]
A pilot trial combining BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment starts.[1]

quick.overview:
BBL, Moxi and Halo are three treatments run on Sciton platforms: broadband light, a light fractional 1927-nm laser and a deeper hybrid fractional laser. Clinics sometimes combine them for pigment, texture and photoaging.

Published work naming them is small, mostly pilot studies and trials with a few dozen participants.
quick.mechanism: BBL uses filtered flashlamp light on pigment and vessels. Moxi and Halo create tiny columns of controlled injury so skin remodels.
quick.risks: Listed concerns include pigment change after laser, healing time with deeper resurfacing, and that these are clinic-only procedures.
